Hello,

That's not what I had in mind. The race condition is theoretical right now, only one goroutine can call `Update` for a single NvidiaDevicePlugin object.

Even if there were multiple goroutines running `HealthCheck()`, this wouldn't solve the problem since `m.devs` is actually updated later. 
Goroutine 1 could read `m.devs` and get `[{dev1, Healthy}, {dev2, Healthy}]`, but then it detects `dev1` is unhealthy thus it calls `m.Update` with `[{dev1, Unhealthy}, {dev2, Healthy}]`. The update is queued in the channel but `m.devs` is unchanged.
After goroutine 1 released the lock, goroutine 2 will also get `[{dev1, Healthy}, {dev2, Healthy}]`. If it detects `dev2` is unhealthy it will call `m.Update` with `[{dev1, Healthy}, {dev2, Unhealthy}]`.

In summary: sending all devices in the `Update` is a bad idea. It should be done per-device, on state change.

I did not enable DevicePlugins feature gate in kubelet.

It requires to edit
```
/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf
```
and add
```
--feature-gates=DevicePlugins=true
```

Maybe it would be good to put a warning into the docs about is.

>  what GPU Allocated memory checks and "Zombie processes" checks do?

Those are related, and it's related to reset too. If it's not possible to reset your card, you at least need to detect when things are broken.

When things go awfully wrong, you can have the following:
* There is no process using the GPU, but `nvidia-smi` shows a non-trivial amount of memory being used. e.g. something like `352MiB / 12181MiB`
* There is a process already using the GPU you are supposed to give to a new container (excluding voluntary sharing). This can happen when there is a GPU fault and the process that had an open CUDA context can't teardown properly.

These kinds of checks are useful safety checks in addition to event-based healthchecks like XIDs and ECCs. Some of these errors could go unnoticed otherwise.

The last `Environment` is re-writing the `KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS` variable you need to merge the two declarations.
Something like: `KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS=--feature-gates=DevicePlugins=true --fail-swap-on=false` should do the trick.

In my case, using OpenShift v3.9 and Docker-ce with Nvidia-p40 GPUs, not like kubernetes-only env(editing kubernetes manifest files in the worker node...)., I had to edit the file '/etc/systemd/system/origin-node.service'

```
### edit "ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker run ..." line
### add "-v /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/:/var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/" line as below
# REDACTED
ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker run --name origin-node \
...
  \
  -v /dev:/dev $DOCKER_ADDTL_BIND_MOUNTS -v /etc/pki:/etc/pki:ro \
  \
  -v /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/:/var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/ \
  \
  openshift/node:${IMAGE_VERSION}
...
``` 

Next, restart origin-node service(on each GPU worker node)

```
# setenforce 0
# systemctl daemon-reload
# systemctl restart origin-node
```

Delete existing k8s-device-plugin daemonset with abnormal status(on master node).
```
# oc delete -f nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset.yml
daemonset "nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset" deleted

Check the yaml for running k8s-device-plugin and re-create the daemonset(on master node).

```
# vi 02-nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset.yml
```
```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset
  namespace: nvidia 
spec:
 template:
   metadata:
     labels:
       name: nvidia-device-plugin-ds
   spec:
     priorityClassName: system-node-critical
     affinity:
       nodeAffinity:
         requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
           nodeSelectorTerms:
           - matchExpressions:
             - key: openshift.com/gpu-accelerator 
               operator: Exists
     securityContext:
        privileged: true
     serviceAccount: nvidia-deviceplugin
     serivceAccountName: nvidia-deviceplugin
     hostNetwork: true
     hostPID: true
     containers:
     - image: nvidia/k8s-device-plugin:1.9
       name: nvidia-device-plugin-ctr
       securityContext:
         allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
         capabilities:
           drop: ["ALL"]
       volumeMounts:
         - name: device-plugin
           mountPath: /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins
     volumes:
       - name: device-plugin
         hostPath:
           path: /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins

`ExtendedResourceToleration` add tolerations, not taints. You added the `taint` yourself, right?

@flx42 Your device plugin needs to tolerate `nvidia.com/gpu` taint so that it can work with `ExtendedResourceToleration`. (Anything which doesn't request GPUs but still need to run on GPU nodes need to tolerate user-added taints)

We made GKE's device plugin tolerate everything (since it's such a critical addon): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.11.2/cluster/addons/device-plugins/nvidia-gpu/daemonset.yaml#L28
@mindprince wait, but does that means the administrator set the `nvidia.com/gpu` taint before deploying the device plugin?
Hm, or I guess that would also happen if the administrator used a `NoExecute` taint, that would evict the device plugin afterwards, right? Is `NoSchedule` insufficient?

We set a `nvidia.com/gpu:NoSchedule` taint while setting up a GPU node pool. So, that nothing gets scheduled on the node. Then device-plugin and driver installer which tolerates all taints run on the node. Similarly kube-proxy, and other critical addons that tolerate all taints run on the node.

Then any GPU pod that requests GPUs can run on the node because the admission controller will tolerate that taint for those pods.

It doesn't harm to add tolerations, but it feels like what you describe is backward. Do you mean you have a special case for GPU nodes when provisioning an instance? I would like to reach a point where GPU nodes are auto-detected, and each container is deployed in the right order automatically: driver container -> device plugin -> monitoring stack. I've started writing some thoughts about this here:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/16FPbc7qtqvJNPlk2sBlYOyhIB9DYXvaUQrEPP4bHmxI/edit?usp=sharing

The device plugin should be the one setting up the `taint` after it has successfully started. An alternative implementation of our device plugin might expose `nvidia.com/vgpu` instead.
With a `NoSchedule` taint it would open the door to CPU jobs starting on this node in parallel with the device plugin initialization. In this case we could use a **different** taint than the extended resource one, for instance a taint that would set by `node-feature-discovery`, before the device driver is even added.

But there is also the question of whether we should be opinionated about this. If we decide to unconditionally taint the node in the device plugin, we are opinionated since we will repel CPU pods and require the deployment of the ExtendedResourceToleration admission controller.
@jeremyeder mentioned they would prefer to use priorities and preemption instead, you would be able to run CPU jobs if there are no GPU jobs pending.

Anyway, I'm getting a bit off-topic and I'm not sure @notnami cares about all this. But the gist is that I don't feel it's a solved problem, and while that's true I don't want to force users to label/taint their nodes (but the toleration should be harmless as I said, we could add it).

CA_CERTIFICATE_FILE_PATH=$CA_CERTIFICATE_DIRECTORY/ca.crt
mkdir -p $CA_CERTIFICATE_DIRECTORY
echo "${aws_eks_cluster.demo.certificate_authority.0.data}" | base64 -d >  $CA_CERTIFICATE_FILE_PATH
INTERNAL_IP=$(curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/local-ipv4)
sed -i s,MASTER_ENDPOINT,${aws_eks_cluster.demo.endpoint},g /var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig
sed -i s,CLUSTER_NAME,${var.cluster-name},g /var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig
sed -i s,REGION,${data.aws_region.current.name},g /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service
sed -i s,MAX_PODS,20,g /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service
sed -i s,MASTER_ENDPOINT,${aws_eks_cluster.demo.endpoint},g /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service
sed -i s,INTERNAL_IP,$INTERNAL_IP,g /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service
DNS_CLUSTER_IP=10.100.0.10
if [[ $INTERNAL_IP == 10.* ]] ; then DNS_CLUSTER_IP=172.20.0.10; fi
sed -i s,DNS_CLUSTER_IP,$DNS_CLUSTER_IP,g /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service
sed -i s,CERTIFICATE_AUTHORITY_FILE,$CA_CERTIFICATE_FILE_PATH,g /var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig
sed -i s,CLIENT_CA_FILE,$CA_CERTIFICATE_FILE_PATH,g  /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart kubelet
USERDATA
}

You should not install the NVIDIA driver inside the container. But you **do** need to install the **CUDA toolkit** libraries (e.g. cuDNN, cuBLAS, cuFFT) inside your container image.

> Assuming I have a subset of my cluster nodes labeled as having nvidia installed and can therefore just target those nodes to run the device plugin, can I get away with just running the nvidia-docker-2.0 on those nodes and plain old docker on all the other nodes?

You can:
- Label your GPU nodes
- Have only your GPU nodes be setup with the nvidia runtime
- Edit the daemonset spec so that the daemonset only runs on nodes with the GPU label

You can set the env variable `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` to `0,1,2,3` in the device plugin spec if you only want it to advertise the first 4 GPUs.

You'll need some more work if you have some nodes with less than 4 GPUs by deploying two device plugins and the clever use of nodeSelectors and labels.

I had a quick look a the sources. [Here](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-runtime/blob/master/hook/nvidia-container-runtime-hook/main.go#L124) the `device` arg of `nvidia-container-cli` gets set. The `Devices` string used there is set [here](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-runtime/blob/master/hook/nvidia-container-runtime-hook/container_config.go#L233). As `getDevices()` uses the environment variable `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, setting this variable as suggested [here](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-docker/wiki/Usage) works around this problem:
```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
spec:
    spec:
      containers:
          env:
            - name: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
              value: "all"
```

I examined the output of journalctl on a on which the GPU count
was zero.  In that log, I observe the following:

```
Nov 13 01:56:55 kube-XXXXX kernel: nvidiafb: HW is currently programmed for CRT^M
Nov 13 01:56:55 kube-XXXXX kernel: nvidiafb: Using CRT on CRTC 0^M
Nov 13 01:56:55 kube-XXXXX kernel: nvidiafb: PCI nVidia NV2 framebuffer (4MB @ 0x5F000000000)^M
Nov 13 01:56:55 kube-XXXXX kernel: NVRM: The NVIDIA probe routine was not called for 4 device(s).^M
Nov 13 01:56:55 kube-XXXXX kernel: NVRM: This can occur when a driver such as: ^M
NVRM: nouveau, rivafb, nvidiafb or rivatv ^M
NVRM: was loaded and obtained ownership of the NVIDIA device(s).^M
Nov 13 01:56:55 kube-XXXXX kernel: NVRM: Try unloading the conflicting kernel module (and/or^M
NVRM: reconfigure your kernel without the conflicting^M
NVRM: driver(s)), then try loading the NVIDIA kernel module^M
NVRM: again.^M
Nov 13 01:56:55 kube-XXXXX kernel: NVRM: No NVIDIA devices probed.^M
```

This shows that first the nvidiafb driver is loaded and is registered to drive
the GPUs, and that second the nvidia driver tries to register to drive the GPUs
and fails to do so because nvidiafb is already registered.  (The resulting
error message explicitly says that the failure can be caused by the presence
of nvidiafb.)

As a result, the nvidia-driver pod, which tried to load the
nvidia driver, fails and does not create the /dev/nvidia* character device
files.The nvidia plugin that supplies kubelet with the count of the available GPUs
counts the /dev/nvidia[0-9]* character device files.  Since the nvidia-driver
pod failed to load the module and did not create the device files, there are
no /dev/nvidia[0-9] device files, so the plugin reports 0 GPUs to kubelet.

This problem seems to be a race between something triggering the automatic loading
of modules and the nvidia-driver pod.  blacklisting the nvidiafb driver should fix this issue.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

from kubernetes import client, config
from kubernetes.client.rest import ApiException
from pprint import pprint
import os
import time

config.load_incluster_config()

api_instance = client.CoreV1Api()
name = 'gpu-config'
namespace = open('/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace').read()
body = client.V1ConfigMap(
    api_version='v1',
    kind='ConfigMap',
    data=dict(NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=os.environ['NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES']),
    metadata=dict(name=name),
)

try:
    api_response = api_instance.replace_namespaced_config_map(name, namespace, body, pretty='true')
    pprint(api_response)
except ApiException as e:
    print('Exception when calling CoreV1Api->replace_namespaced_config_map: %s\n' % e)

print('Sleeping forever')

while True:

Forget everything I said before. The following is what I should have told you in the first place.

If you want to use K8s with docker 19.03 and GPUs, you need to continue using `nvidia-docker2`, not  just `nvidia-container-toolkit`. 

That said, `nvidia-docker2` was recently rearchitected to simply wrap `nvidia-container-toolkit` with a thin wrapper to serve as the `nvidia-container-runtime` that you need to set in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`.

All this wrapper does is take the runc spec as input, inject the `nvidia-container-runtime-hook` as a prestart hook and call out to the native `runc`, passing it the modfied runc spec with that hook set. Moreover, the `nvidia-container-runtime-hook` is now just a symlink to `nvidia-container-toolkit`.

So you are basically running on the exact same stack as you would be whether you install `nvidia-docker2` or `nvidia-container-toolkit`, except that `nvidia-docker2` will install a thin runtime for you that you can set in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`.

It does not implement QoS or memory pools.  It is more akin to how users use a shared server with GPUs but it does limit the oversubscription.   So there is risk that you will clobber someone else, however it is unlikely when users are sporadically using the GPU (due to statistical multiplexing), for example when multiple pods want to share a GPU for model serving with infrequent requests.  Besides, users opt-in to the shared GPUs by setting the nvidia.com/sharedgpu=1 (instead of nvidia.com/gpu where they would get exclusive access).

When the number of replicas for the GPUs is set to 1, the approach is equivalent to what you have currently (i.e. exclusive access).  Supporting both nvidia.com/gpu (exclusive) and nvidia.com/sharedgpu (shared) on the same cluster is what I am doing right now.

Hi @zvonkok,

I agree that this is strange and unexpected for nodes that have GPUs on them. However, the plugin was designed so that it could land on non-GPU nodes (e.g. in a mixed cluster) and avoid sitting in a constant restart loop.

That said, it sits on an empty `select {}` loop when it reaches this condition, so you can always send it a `SIGTERM` via `docker exec` to force it to restart once you know the driver is installed, something like:
```
docker exec <plugin-pod> kill -SIGTERM 1
```

> What about adding a script that does a restart internally in the Pod rather than having k8s scheduler doing that?

We already run a restart loop internally for connection errors with the kubelet (which typically result from the a kubelet upgrade or the kubelet being duty cycled to swap some command line flags).

DaemonSet(s) are not made for running to completion and we are trying here to implement such a solution.

I had the same issue setting up a k8s cluster with GPUs. Went through the comments here and other related issues, and put together the steps to make it work, probably useful to people looking for solution:

### Kubernetes NVIDIA GPU device plugin

- follow the [official NVIDIA GPU device plugin](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-gpus/scheduling-gpus/#official-nvidia-gpu-device-plugin) until the step to configure runtime
- as explained in [this comment](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/issues/168#issuecomment-625966602), k8s still needs `nvidia-container-runtime`; install it:
  ```bash
  # install the old nvidia-container-runtime for k8s
  curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/nvidia-container-runtime/gpgkey | \
    sudo apt-key add -
  distribution=$(. /etc/os-release;echo $ID$VERSION_ID)
  curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/nvidia-container-runtime/$distribution/nvidia-container-runtime.list | \
    sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-runtime.list
  sudo apt-get update
  sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-container-runtime
  ```

- add the following /etc/docker/daemon.json as required by k8s
  ```json
  {
      "default-runtime": "nvidia",
      "runtimes": {
          "nvidia": {
              "path": "/usr/bin/nvidia-container-runtime",
              "runtimeArgs": []
          }
      }
  }
  ```

- restart docker and test:
  ```bash
  sudo systemctl restart docker
  # test that docker can run with GPU without the --gpus flag
  docker run nvidia/cuda:10.2-runtime-ubuntu18.04 nvidia-smi
  ```

- finally, install the NVIDIA device plugin on your cluster:
  ```bash
  kubectl create -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/1.0.0-beta4/nvidia-device-plugin.yml
  ```

I finally got some time to finish reading @klueska plan in the links above.  The plan is to only support A100 GPUs with CUDA 11  by supporting pre-determined fixed slices (memory and compute) of GPUs.  The different sized slices would be allocated as different resource types in k8s.  This sounds like a good plan for fixed slices without sharing memory and compute.

The modifications I made to the nvidia device plugin solve a slightly different problem.  There are cases when you do not need guaranteed GPU availability.  For example, when you are interactively experimenting in ML (think Jupyter Hub) you actually want access to all the GPU memory and all the compute resources but you might only need it for a few seconds or a few minutes and then you free them up (stop computing and free the memory).  Another user on the same system can kick off their test and all is good.  We can even have multiple users running their tests at the same time so long as they do not exceed the total amount of memory on the GPU.

I think there are strong use cases for both and in fact both solutions can co-exist with each other.  For example you can have a parameter to create replicas of the GPU **slices** to allow sharing at the GPU slice level if desired.

Regarding the questions from https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/issues/180#issuecomment-642014373, the [`v0.7.0-rc.1`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/tree/v0.7.0-rc.1) release has opted for the following:

> 1) How useful do people find exposing all 4 strategies listed in [Supporting Multi-Instance GPUs (MIG) in Kubernetes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1mdgMQ8g7WmaI_XVVRrCvHPFPOMCm5LQD5JefgAh6N8g).
> 2) Could we get away with having just 2 strategies (i.e. **single** and **mixed**), where **mixed** refers to what is currently called **mixed-fully-qualified**.

We have decided to only support 2 strategies: **single** and **mixed**. These two strategies solve the use cases for 95% of the users out there. We can revisit supporting the **mixed-memory-qualified** and **mixed-fractionally-qualified** strategies in the future if demand for them arises again.

> 3) How do people feel about the way MIG devices are being passed back over the plugin API via environment variables of the form `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES_*`.
>
>    This leverages an alpha feature in the NVIDIA container toolkit that allows one to merge all of these back into a single `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` variable.
>
>    This makes it easy to have each resource type in the **mixed** strategies to add devices to the `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` environment variable, but it also means that there is no easy way to _override_ this variable via a webhook or other means to prevent people from bypassing the `k8s-device-plugin` altogether.

We have decided not leverage the use of this "merging" environment variable feature.

However, this comes with some weirdness / limitations when running under the `mixed` strategy:
1) Only **one** device type can be requested by a container at a time. If more than one device type is requested, it is __undefined__ which one the container will actually get access to. For example, a container cannot request *both* an `nvidia.com/gpu` and an `nvidia.com/mig-3g.20gb` at the same time. However, it can request multiple instances of the same resource type (e.g. `nvidia.com/gpu: 2` or `nvidia.com/mig-3g.20gb: 2`) without problems.
2) If you do happen to request multiple resource types, kubernetes will still allocate / bill all of the resources to your container. You just wont be able to see / access any of them except one.

In practice, this shouldn't be a problem because CUDA wouldn't be able to leverage more than one of these resource types at a time anyway. That said, we plan to fix this problem by the time the full `v0.7.0` release of this plugin becomes available. So stay tuned.

A partial answer to your question is here:
https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin#versioning

The gist of it is the following though:
1) Before Kubernetes v1.10 the versioning scheme of the device plugin had to match exactly the version of Kubernetes. This is  why you see tags for v1.8, v1.9, v1.10, v1.11, v1.12 in the device plugin (we kept this versioning scheme all the way to v1.12 even though it wasn't technically necessary).
2) As mentioned [here](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin#version-v000), we eventually moved to SEMVER since the release of the plugin no longer needed to be tied to the version of K8s it was being run on. When we first made this change, the version scheme used was of the format `1.0.0-beta*`. This continued from `1.0.0-beta0` - `1.0.0-beta6`.
3) This versioning scheme had issues, however, because there was no easy way to produce a `pre-release` of the plugin before releasing a more stable version later on. It left users of the plugin constantly wondering if the latest plugin should be considered production ready or not.
3) To address this, we changed the versioning scheme as part of the `1.0.0-beta6` release to move away from the `1.0.0-beta*` scheme in favor of what you see today (i.e. `v0.x.x`). With this new scheme we are now able to produce `pre-releases` (e.g. `v0.7.0-rc.5`) that early adopters can consume before the final stable version is released (e.g. `v0.7.0`).
4) So as not to break existing users we kept the labels for `1.0.0-beta` - `1.0.0-beta6`, but mapped them as follows (`1.0.0-beta`--> `v0.0.0`, `1.0.0-beta1`--> `v0.1.0`, `1.0.0-beta´2`--> `v0.2.0`, `1.0.0-beta3`--> `v0.3.0`, `1.0.0-beta4`--> `v0.4.0`, `1.0.0-beta5`--> `v0.5.0`, `1.0.0-beta6`--> `v0.6.0`).

I hope this clears things up -- at least for how the versioning works, and why the set of tags exist as they do.

Hi @Jeffwan 

> I see in the design doc you mentioned it needs to cut any GPU connections to switch into/out of MIG mode. Seems you just remove device plugin and gpu feature discovery and restart kubelet. Does machine really need to be restarted?

If you are running in a VM (i.e. using GPU pass through virtualization), then the VM really does need to be restarted. If you are running on bare-metal then you can technically just remove all connections to the GPU and issue a GPU reset. However, enumerating all of the services that have connections to the GPU can sometimes be tricky. In the K8s stack you only have the plugin, GFD, and the kubelet itself. There may be other services running on the machine (e.g. nvidia-persistenced) that also need to be stopped and started somehow.

In theory, it _is_ possible to enumerate all of these, stop them, put the GPU into MIG mode, and restart them all. However, since a reboot is required in the VM case anyway (and the fact that this is a very infrequent operation), we've been tending to recommend a reboot in all cases.

> Another question is once the A100 is in MIG mode, GIs and CIs can be configured dynamically. I assume user needs to remove and reinstall device plugin and gpu feature discovery right? In this case, I think we don't need to reboot machine or kubelet?

That is correct. You don't need to reboot in this case. You don't need to remove and reinstall the device plugin or GFD either. GFD will automatically pick up the change after a delay of about 10 seconds. The plugin will need to be reinitialized, but you don't technically need to restart it. Sending it a SIGHUP signal should be enough (i.e. `kubectl exec <plugin-pod-id> -- kill -SIGHUP 1`).

> In AWS, most user use ASG to manage their kubernetes node groups. I feel like there's no good ways to reboot the machines. Technically, user can either put the instance to standby or suspend the health check process but seems to complicated and manual. So any suggestions on daily operation?

This is definitely a case of running in a VM (so requires a reboot in all cases). I haven't personally looked into this, but I know NVIDIA is still working with Amazon to figure out the best way to support MIG on AWS. I will make sure they are aware of this issue with using ASGs and see what their suggestions are.

The good news is that the next generation of GPUs is being designed to *not* require a GPU reset to be put into MIG mode. Unfortunately, we will have to live with it for the A100 series, but this problem should go away in future generations.

The current recommendation for setting up MIG on a GPU (that is already in MIG mode) involves:

* Drain the GPU of any currently running jobs (using a taint of some sort)
* Perform the reconfiguration
* Restart the device plugin (either duty-cycle it or send it a SIGHUP signal)
* Remove the taint

Unfortunately, there are no device-level taints, so setting up MIG on a GPU will require draining the whole node of jobs, and not just an individual GPU. This is likely OK in practice, since this should be a fairly infrequent operation. However, it would be nice to have support for something like device-level taints in the future.

We are currently looking to put together an operator to ensure the order of these operations is honored during reconfiguration (but we are still in the early design phase). I've seen recently that some third-party vendors put one together already (https://github.com/riskfuel/k8s-mig-operator), but there is no officially sponsored one from NVIDIA yet.

This is not a property of the k8s-decive-plugin, but rather of the underlying `nvidia-container-toolkit` (which does the job of injecting `libnvidia*` into all containers for you -- including the k8s-device-plugin container).

You can configure where it looks for the driver under `/etc/nvidia-container-runtime/config.toml` with the following option:

#root = "/run/nvidia/driver"

I expect to create a pod successfully regardless of the image, only using `nividia.com/gpu` to controll the num of GPU, without knowing the NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES env.

But today I need to know whether the image has NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES env. Or I need to unset NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES if I don't want GPU when using ngc image.

If you actually ask for some `nvidia.com/gpu` resources, then it doesn't matter if the image has `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` set or not -- it will be ignored, and the volume-mounts set up by the plugin will be used instead.

It's only a problem in the case where you attempt to launch an NGC container (which has `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` set by default), but you *don't* request any `nvidia.com/gpu` resources (so the plugin is never invoked and no volume mounts are set up / `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is not overwritten by the plugin). In this case you will get the error you are seeing because the system thinks you are trying to request GPUs via the envvar, but don't have the correct permissions to do so.

The only way to address the issue you are seeing would be to change the underlying `nvidia-container-toolkit` to silently ignore `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` if a container does not have the proper permissions to use it to control which GPUs get injected. There is no way to do this from the plugin because it does not get invoked in the case where no `nvidia.com/gpu` resources are requested. 

I agree this is a bit unintutive, but I'm not 100% sure what the right semantics should be at the moment.
At the very least we should print a warning in the nvidi-container-toolkit log if this occurs, but maybe it makes sense to not error out as it's doing today.

Let me think  about this a bit more and I'll report back here on what we can.

At present, all CUDA cleints (of which tensorflow is one) can only make use of a single MIG device at a time (because there is no P2P communication possible between MIG devices). It will simply pick up and use the first one it finds, ignoring all others.

Yes, I can confirm that this is an issue.

MIG support in the `k8s-device-plugin` was tested together with the `compatWithCPUManager` when it first came out and it worked just fine. However, since that time, the way that the underlying GPU driver exposes MIG to a container has changed. It was originally based on something called `/proc` based `nvidia-capabilities` and now it's based on something called `/dev` based `nvidia-capabilities` (more info on this [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/194A-Hg3mLlIW4eo2BSUcGKpzZf2ciX47eoH5T-WZNXo/edit?ts=5fd54b8c)).

Without going into too much detail, when the underlying driver switched its implementation for this, it broke `compatWithCPUManager` in the `k8s-device-plugin` when MIG is enabled.

The fix should be fairly straightforward and will involve listing out the set of device nodes associated with the `nvidia-capabibilities` that grant access to the MIG device being allocated -- and sending them back to the kubelet (the same way the device nodes for full GPUs are sent back [here](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/blob/master/server.go#L284)).

I have added this to our list of tasks for `v0.8.0` which will be released sometime in January.

In the meantime, if you need this to work today, you can follow the advice in ["Working with nvidia-capabilities"
](https://docs.google.com/document/d/194A-Hg3mLlIW4eo2BSUcGKpzZf2ciX47eoH5T-WZNXo/edit?ts=5fd54b8c) and flip your driver settings from `/dev` based `nvidia-capabilities` to `/proc` based `nvidia-capabilities` via:
```
$ modprobe nvidia nv_cap_enable_devfs=0
```

That should get things working again until a fix come out. It is not a long-term fix, however, as support for `/proc` based `nvidia-capabilities` will disappear in a future driver release.

I've looked into this a bit more. The `Allocatable` field is not meant to be a "real-time" count of the resources available in the cluster. The naming is obviously confusing, but here's how `Allocatable` is calculated:
```
   [Allocatable] = [Node Capacity] - [Kube-Reserved] - [System-Reserved] - [Hard-Eviction-Threshold]
```
This can be seen in:
https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/node/node-allocatable.md#api-changes.

For GPUs (and probably most other devices with a plugin), this means that `Allocatable` will always equal to `Capacity` so long as all devices remain healthy.

The `Allocatable` count will only go down if the plugin decides to report fewer devices on the persistent `ListAndWatch()` connection that it maintains with the `kubelet`.  The kubelet will track *all* of the devices it has ever received from `ListAndWatch()`, marking those *not* contained in the most recent list as "unhealthy". The `Capacity` will then be reported as the total number of devices it has ever seen, and `Allocatable` will be reported as the number of healthy ones in this list (i.e. the count of the devices contained in the most recent list sent to the kubelet).

In this way (for device plugins) you can think of these two values as:
1. `Capacity`: The number of (healthy + unhealthy) devices
1. `Allocatable`: The number of (healthy) devices

If you really want to deploy it on *all* nodes (and just have it sit on a blocked state on non-GPU nodes), then you can set the `failOniInitError` flag to `false` when deploying it.

Due to GPL reasons, the NVIDIA kernel driver is not allowed to create `/dev` nodes in user-space.
A separate binary called `nvidia-modprobe` is shipped with the driver that can be invoked from userspace to create the necessary `/dev` nodes on your behalf.

To create the `/dev/nvidia-uvm*` ones, the relevant command is:
```
nvidia-modprobe -u -c=0
```

To create the `/dev/nvidia-modeset` device, the relevant command is:
```
/usr/bin/nvidia-modprobe -m
```

To create the `/dev/nvidia*` devices corresponding to actual GPUs, the relevant command is:
```
/usr/bin/nvidia-modprobe -c <gpu-minor>
```

The preferred method to invoke this program to create these `/dev` nodes on your host is via `nvidia-persistenced`. You can set this up as a service running on our system to ensure that all GPU devices are available at all times. Please see:
https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/driver-persistence/index.html#persistence-daemon

That said, I'm surprised that the `device-plugin` doesn't see the `/dev/nvidia-modeset` or `/dev/nvidia-uvm*` devices because `libnvidia-container` should make sure they are created and available inside any container that is launched by the `nvidia-container-runtime` (which the device plugin definitely is).

Here is the relevant code:
https://github.com/NVIDIA/libnvidia-container/blob/master/src/nvc.c#L205
https://github.com/NVIDIA/libnvidia-container/blob/master/src/nvc.c#L213

Can you show me your settings for `libnvidia-container` under `/etc/nvidia-container-runtime/config.toml`?
If you have `load-kmods = false`, then this might explain things.
And if you have it set to that (and you want to keep it that way), then you will need to make sure the appropriate `nvidia-modprobe` commands are called on your host system at bootup (either manually or via `nvidia-persistenced`).

The only way to do that is to deploy 2 separate daemonsets. 
One daemonset with NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set one way and another daemonset with it set another way.

You then need to make sure and apply appropriate labels to the nodes which should have each variant, and use a `nodeSelector` in your daemonset spec to direct each daemonset to the appropriate set of nodes.

Hi @srstrickland. What is the value of `NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES` in the container? I would assume that this should at least include `compute` for a TensorFlow image.

Note that the toolkit is only designed to mount driver libraries and the expectation is that runtime libraries or other components of the SDK such as CUDNN / CUBLAS are included in the container. This is the reason that it is required to mount these libraries from the host if they are not present.

Note, one of the things that libnvidia-container does under the hood is to update the ldcache in the container. As such, ensuring that the mounted folder is in the ldcache path should remove the need to set the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` as the cache would be updated accordingly.

Yes, the device plugin makes the Kubernetes scheduler aware of gpu resources in your cluster. In your example, you manually did this. The major advantage of the device plugin is that it automates this process for all nodes and allows you to scale up/down your cluster seamlessly.

We've seen this issue popping up on some people's setups but do not have a diagnosis yet. In general this can happen if some component on your system is calling `Update()` against your container, causing it to lose access to the cgroups associated with the GPUs.

It's possible it is linked to an issue that was recently fixed in `runC`:
https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/2366#issue-609480075

This bug causes every update to a container's devices cgroup to temporarily block access to *all* devices before applying the update (even if there is no change in permissions). If a GPU was accessed during this small time window, you would see the error you are describing.

That said, we've seen this issue pop up even on systems with a version of `runC` that fixes this bug, so it's not 100% conclusive.

The only thing we've seen that fully resolves the issue is to upgrade to an "experimental" version of our NVIDIA container runtime that bypasses the need for libnvidia-container to change cgroup permissions out from underneath `runC`.

For older versions of kubernetes, yes, the `cadvisor` linked into the kubelet is a GPU client and there is no way to turn that off. You have to bring down the kubelet in order to change MIG mode. That said, simply changing MIG configurations does *not* require you to bring down all GPU clients (only changing MIG mode). So you can change to MIG mode once, and then reconfigure it as many times as you like without bringing down the kubelet.

We have a K8s component (called the `k8s-mig-manager`) that orchestrates all of this for you, but it is currently only designed to work with the GPU operator: https://github.com/NVIDIA/mig-parted/tree/main/deployments/gpu-operator

Kubernetes 1.24 switched from dockershim as the default CRI provider to containerd. That means you either need to explicitly configure your kubelet to run with an alternate dockershim or configure containerd to use the nvidia-container-runtime as its default runtime (similar to how you used to have to do for docker).

> Kubernetes 1.24 переключился с dockershim в качестве поставщика CRI по умолчанию на containerd. Это означает, что вам нужно либо явно настроить kubelet для работы с альтернативным dockershi, либо настроить containerd для использования nvidia-container-runtime в качестве среды выполнения по умолчанию (аналогично тому, как вы делали это раньше для docker).

Regarding your second question -- it shouldn't matter much between
```
runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"
```
and
```
runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v1"
```
Modern containerds come with the `io.containerd.runc.v2` shim, but this wasn't always true, so `io.containerd.runc.v1` was used to make sure the instructions worked even on older containerds.
This was addressed in https://gitlab.com/nvidia/kubernetes/device-plugin/-/merge_requests/200

I'm not exactly sure what you mean (maybe you can rephrase the question), but GPU memory is similar to CPU memory in that:

1. There is a fixed amount of it
2. It can be allocated into a virtual address space for private use by each process
4. It must explicitly be freed in order to make it available for others to use

The main difference being that there is no swap out to disk if you try and allocate beyond the limits of the physical memory. The system will just return an OutOfMemory error and your process will crash.

@devriesewouter89 note that `k3s` uses a speicific `containerd` config template and configures the NVIDIA Container Runtime if this is installed on the system at startup. Note that this doesn't set the default runtime. One option is to use a `RuntimeClass` when launching pods that are supposed to use have access to GPUs.

Note that looking at the initial logs that you provided you may have been using `v1.7.0` of the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. This is quite an old version and we greatly improved our support for Tegra-based systems with the `v1.10.0` release. It should also be noted that in order to use the GPU Device Plugin on Tegra-based systems (specifically targetting the integrated GPUs) at least `v1.11.0` of the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is required.

There are no Tegra-specific changes in the `v1.12.0` release, so using the `v1.11.0` release should be sufficient in this case.

Set `device-id-strategy` to `index` did not solve the UUID  change issue due VM migration completely. Although env `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` for containers is set to index of allocated GPU cards, UUID is still reported to kubelet which caches these infomation in the `kubelet_internal_checkpoint` file. And then kubelet still use UUID to find and allocate GPU to containers. In the following case for a node with 2 GPU cards, it's possible to allocate 2 containers to the same card, and leave the other one vacant but unassignable:
A pod  with one container, C1,  requesting one GPU, is created and scheduled to a node, N1,  with 2 GPUs. kubelet allocates GPU #0 to C1. 
Later the baremetal machine underlying N1 has problem and N1 is migrated to another baremetal. After migration, N1 starts and C1 is recreated and resumes running. For now, the`RegisteredDevices`field in checkpoint file contains new UUIDs which do not include the UUID of  `DeviceIDs` allocated to C1. 
Now a new pod with contaier C2,   requesting one GPU, is created and scheduled to N1. Since kubelet can't find the allocated UUID to C1 , it's possible that kubelet allocates GPU #0 AGAIN to C2. In result, C1 and C2 both use GPU #0.

With this PR, when `device-id-strategy` set to `index`, indexes, instead of UUIDs will be reported to kubelet and informations in checkpoint file looks likes this `"RegisteredDevices":{"nvidia.com/gpu":["0","1"]}`.

I have just released `nvshare`, a transparent GPU sharing mechanism **without memory size constraints**, based on my diploma thesis.

- With `nvshare` you can concurrently run multiple processes/containers on the same GPU safely, each process/container having the **whole physical GPU memory available**.
- `nvshare` doesn't impose any memory limit for containers and respects security (unlike for example MPS), as each container runs in its own CUDA context, unchanged.
- The GPU memory between processes/containers/Pods is fully isolated, as they have **distinct page tables**.

You can check it out at https://github.com/grgalex/nvshare

Note that using the CTR comman: `ctr run --rm --gpus 0 -t docker.io/nvidia/cuda:12.1.1-runtime-ubuntu20.04 n nvidia-smi` is not sufficient in this case since this uses a different mechanism for injecting the devices (by adding the `nvidia-container-runtime-hook` directly) from the Device plugin.

@inecup this indicates that an `Xid=44` and `Xid=33` critical errors were detected by NVML (see https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/xid-errors/index.html). The device(s) with which these error are asociated are marked as unhealthy by the device plugin so that they cannot be allocated for workloads.

Once the errors are resolved (e.g. by resetting the device), the device plugin can be restarted to mark the device as healthy once more.

Hi @kwohlfahrt. The CDI mode in the plugin was introduced to be used in the context of the GPU Operator. Although it is theoretically possible to use this standalone, this is not something that we've documented at present.

One issue is that the device plugin also needs access to NVIDIA devices and libraries to enumerate the available GPUs. In the context of the GPU operator we configure the NVIDIA Container Runtime as a runtime in the cri-o (or Containerd) config and then launch the device plugin using a runtime class associated with this runtime. This allows the Device Plugin to have the required access to generate the CDI specifications that can be used in CDI-enabled runtimes. In this case the hook you mention is then not needed.

Note that at present, in order to enable CDI mode, the `deviceListStrategy` must include `cdi-annotations` -- which is not the case in your applied config.

Because the NVIDIA driver is not GPL compatible, the kernel driver cannot create these device files for you, and some mechanism in user-space must always do this.

If you install the NVIDIA driver through standard packages on e.g. Ubuntu, `udev` rules are put in place to handle this for you. If you run on  different distribution, or install the NVIDIA driver from its `.run` file, you have to take care of this yourself.

As you point out, running nvidia-smi is another way to trigger creation of these device nodes, as that is something initiated in user-space that has the ability to create the nodes for you.

Adding the taint for `kubectl taint nodes kind-control-plane gpu:NoSchedule` is what made the daemonset no longer schedulable on the control plane node. If you want it to be scheduled there you should not add this taint.

kubectl taint nodes kind-control-plane nvidia.com/gpu:NoSchedule
```

I verified the staging image`registry.gitlab.com/nvidia/kubernetes/device-plugin/staging/k8s-device-plugin:8b416016` that it is truely working on wsl2.

## Based on dockerd
Step 1, install k3s cluster based on dockerd
```bash
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -s - --docker
```

Step 2, install dp with the staging image.
```bash
# set RuntimeClass
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: nvidia
handler: docker
EOF

# install nvdp
helm repo add nvdp https://nvidia.github.io/k8s-device-plugin
helm upgrade -i nvdp nvdp/nvidia-device-plugin \
    --namespace nvdp \
    --create-namespace \
    --set=runtimeClassName=nvidia \
    --set=image.repository=registry.gitlab.com/nvidia/kubernetes/device-plugin/staging/k8s-device-plugin \
    --set=image.tag=8b416016
```

## Based on containerd
Step 1, install k3s cluster based on containerd
```bash
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -
```

Step 2, install dp with the staging image.
```bash
# set RuntimeClass
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: nvidia
handler: nvidia # change the handler to `nvidia` for containerd
EOF

# install nvdp with the same steps as above.
```

## Test with nvdp
```bash
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: gpu-pod
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  runtimeClassName: nvidia
  containers:
    - name: cuda-container
      image: nvcr.io/nvidia/k8s/cuda-sample:vectoradd-cuda10.2
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1 # requesting 1 GPU
  tolerations:
  - key: nvidia.com/gpu

EOF
```

The primary issue here is that the device plugin is started in privileged mode to have access to the device nodes for enumeration. This means that the `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` environment variable has no effect -- except that it ensures that the required libraries for enumerating the devices are mounted into the container.

Allowing for a set of devices to be selected for use with the device plugin is something that we have discussed internally, but we don't have a timeline or concrete plan of implementation.

If you pre-deploy `node-feature-discovery`, then you will need to disable its auto-deployment via the `device-plugin` (otherwise it will likely cause conflicts):

i.e.
```
helm upgrade -i nvdp nvdp/nvidia-device-plugin     \
    --version=0.14.1     \
    --debug --reset-values     \
    --namespace nvidia-device-plugin     \
    --create-namespace     \
    --set gfd.enabled=true.    \
    --set nfd.enabled=false
```

That said, the version of `node-feature-discovery` that is launched automatically by the `device-plugin` is the only one it is tested against, so pre-deploying your own may cause other unforeseen issues.

I'm assuming you use `containerd` as your runtime for kubernetes, not docker (`containerd` is the default).

Meaning you need to configure `containerd` to work with the `nvidia-container-toolkit`:
```
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=containerd --set-as-default
```

Instructions for reference:
https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/container-toolkit/latest/install-guide.html#configuring-containerd

I added the additional `--set-as-default` flag since that is how you had configured docker as well.

> There is still no planned support for this in the k8s-device plugin

Is there a reason why this isn't planned to be implemented here? This seems like an essential feature for any cluster with more than 1 model of GPU and there's currently no adequate workaround at all.

It was a product decision, not an engineering one.

All of the code to support it is merged in the plugin and simply disabled by https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/blob/main/cmd/nvidia-device-plugin/main.go#L239.

The decision not to support this gets revisited periodically, but our product team is still not in favor of it, so our hands are tied.

If you want to enable it in a custom build of the plugin, just remove that line referenced above and it should work as described in https://docs.google.com/document/d/1dL67t9IqKC2-xqonMi6DV7W2YNZdkmfX7ibB6Jb-qmk/edit#heading=h.jw5js7865egx.

apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass

  name: nvidia

spec:
  restartPolicy: OnFailure
  runtimeClassName: nvidia

## A couple of notes for the gpu-operator

### Labels

Nvidia GPU operator requires a manual label: `feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present=true` for [node-feature-discovery](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/node-feature-discovery) to add all necessary labels for the GPU operator to work. This applies only to `kind` and `qbo` not sure why `k8s` requires more labels as indicated here https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/issues/332#issuecomment-1649468259


The label can be added as follows:

```
for i in $(kubectl get no --selector '!node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' -o json | jq -r '.items[].metadata.name'); do
        kubectl label node $i feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present=true
done
```

The reson is that WSL2 doesn't contains PCI info under `/sys` and [node-feature-discovery](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/node-feature-discovery) is unable detect the GPU 

I believe the relevant code is here: [node-feature-discovery/source/usb/utils.go:106](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/node-feature-discovery/blob/master/source/pci/pci.go)

I believe `node-feature-discovery` is expecting something like the output below to build `10de` label

```
lspci -nn |grep -i  nvidia
0000:01:00.0 VGA compatible controller [0300]: NVIDIA Corporation GA106M [GeForce RTX 3060 Mobile / Max-Q] [10de:2560] (rev a1)
0000:01:00.1 Audio device [0403]: NVIDIA Corporation Device [10de:228e] (rev a1)
```

I believe the right place to add this label is once the driver has been detected in the host. See here

https://gitlab.com/nvidia/kubernetes/gpu-operator/-/merge_requests/881/diffs

I'll add my comments there.

@yizhouv5 the device plugin reacts to a subset of NVML events that are associated with critical Xid errors: https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/blob/7e6e3765be7414717b8a8e3972cd936cccc9384a/internal/rm/health.go#L94

We also have a filter that skips a list of errors that are considered application and not device errors: https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/blob/7e6e3765be7414717b8a8e3972cd936cccc9384a/internal/rm/health.go#L65-L71

There are however errors that do not trigger the NVML events that we are known not to handle. Xid 119, for example. There is work on our backlog to improve the error handling of the plugin, but we don't have a clear timeline of when this will be addressed.

With regards to "simulating" failures or marking GPUs as explicitly unhealty, we don't have a mechanism to do this at present. ```
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=containerd --set-as-default

```

Note that if you don't want to set the `nvidia` runtime as default, you can also leave off the `--set-as-default` flag and use a runtime class to launch GPU jobs.

We are aware of a similar, yet slightly different issue with GFD support on DGX-Station machines. Our plan for the next release is to completely filter out all DISPLAY devices, and only support COMPUTE devices in our enumeration of GPUs for both the device plugin and GFD. In the future, we may decide to support DISPLAY devices, but at that point they would show up as a different type of allocatable device (e.g. `nvidia.com/display` instead of `nvidia.com/gpu`), and the labels applied by GFD would reflect this similarly (i.e. `nvidia.com/display.product` and `nvidia.com/display.replicas`, etc.).

To add more context, SkyPilot is a tool for running ML workloads on clouds, and more recently Kubernetes. Our users specifically select a GPU type (e.g., A100, L4, V100) and then SkyPilot runs the task on the requested GPUs. Since for us, these GPU types are non-fungible, (e.g., users choose their hyperparameters depending on what GPU type they will run their job on, costs are different etc), we cannot use compute capability or memory as a filter for choosing which GPU to run on and must select based on GPU type.

We just change the vGPU device code in our environment. If it fails to get the vendor specific capability, return a warning instead of an error. So that it can run in non-privileged mode with an empty vGPU list. Thus we don't need the `--no-vgpu-labels` argument. Is this an acceptable solution?

```diff
$ diff internal/vgpu/vgpu.go.orig internal/vgpu/vgpu.go
21a22,23
> 
>   "k8s.io/klog/v2"
76c78,79
<                       return nil, fmt.Errorf("unable to read vendor specific capability for %s: %v", device.Address, err)
---
>                       klog.Warningf("unable to read vendor specific capability for %s: %v", device.Address, err)
>                       continue
```
That is definitely a simpler solution. @klueska @cdesiniotis do you have any problems with not failing labels if VGPU info cannot be detected?

You're right in pointing out that the issue is that the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and its component are not available by default on GKE systems. This means that the logic to inject the required devices and libraries into the GFD container (based on the content of the `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` environment variable is never triggered.

Note that it's not a requirement that Docker be used, and Containerd (which I understand is used in this context) can be configured to use the NVIDIA Container Runtime as a runtime. If you're able to modify the containerd config on your nodes, this may be an option. The NVIDIA Container Runtime can be configured in containerd and as a runtime class in k8s. If the GFD pod is started using this runtime class, then it should have access to the required devices.

I don't have any more concrete answers as to when this will be addressed, but we are aware of the different experience on GKE and are working to address it. For now, since the driver files -- including `libnvidia-ml.so.1` -- are available at a well-known location on the host and consumed by the [device plugin used on GKE](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/container-engine-accelerators). It may be possible to modify your GFD configuration to also have access to these file so that they can be found.
